sections.body:
This is a story about Bo the bear. Bo is big, warm and brown. Bo lives in a cave with a wooden door.

A good story has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle, and an end. The beginning tells you who the characters are. The middle brings a problem. The end fixes the problem in a way you did not expect.

This story has that shape. In the beginning, Bo keeps all the honey. In the middle, Bo says no to every friend. In the end, Bo learns what his friends have been giving him all along.

The animals in this story talk in short, warm sentences. Read them aloud if you can. A story told out loud is a story you remember.

Listen first. Then tell the story back to someone. That is how a story becomes yours.
examples: This story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
Bo is the bear, and he keeps all the honey.
I can tell this story again tomorrow.
sections.heading: What this story is about

sections.body:
Bo the bear has twelve pots of honey. They are golden and they are heavy.

He made them himself. He counted them every morning. He counted them every evening. Twelve pots, and every one of them was his.

Autumn comes. The leaves turn yellow. The bees go home to sleep. The meadows turn brown.

Bo's friends come to visit. First comes Foxy, who is cold and hungry. Then comes Rabbit, who has nothing but carrots. Then comes little Wren the bird, who has nothing at all.

They each want one pot of honey. Just one little pot.

But Bo says no. Every time. His honey is his honey.
examples: Bo has twelve golden pots of honey.
The bees go home to sleep in autumn.
Bo says no to every friend.
sections.heading: The beginning: twelve golden pots

sections.body:
Then winter comes. It is a hard winter. The snow is deep and the wind is cold.

Bo's cave is warm, but there is no honey left. He ate the last pot in October. The pots are empty and they are all his.

Bo goes out looking for food. He digs for roots. He waits by the stream. He finds nothing.

Bo comes back to his cave at night. He is tired. He is hungry. He feels sorry for himself.

But then he hears a knock on his wooden door.

It is Foxy. And Foxy is not alone.
examples: The snow is deep and the wind is cold.
Bo's honey pots are all empty.
There is a knock on the wooden door.
sections.heading: The middle: the winter that comes

sections.body:
Foxy carries a small pot of honey. Rabbit carries a pot too. And Wren the bird has one, hidden in her feathers.

They put the pots down on Bo's floor.

Foxy says: you kept your honey last autumn, and now we share ours.

Bo does not understand at first. He looks at the three little pots. Then Bo looks at the door. Then Bo looks at his own twelve empty pots.

And Bo understands. His friends did not take from him. They gave to him, again and again, and he never noticed.

Bo opens the door wide. He asks all his friends inside. Bo shares his food, and there is not much of it, but there is enough.

From that day, Bo keeps two pots for his friends. And he says yes more often than he says no.
examples: You kept your honey, and now we share ours.
His friends gave to him, and he never noticed.
From that day, Bo says yes more often.
sections.heading: The surprise: the door opens, and the honey comes in

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in this story. Learn them here, and you can use them in your own sentences.

Honey is the sweet golden food that bees make. Bees collect it from flowers.

A **den** is the home of a bear. It is a cave with a door, and it is warm inside.

To **share** means to give part of what you have to someone else, and to let them have some too.

Jealous describes the sad feeling you get when someone else has something you want. It is a feeling, not a plan.

A **friend** is someone who is glad to see you, even when you have nothing to give.
examples: Honey is the sweet golden food that bees make.
To share means to give some of what you have.
A friend is glad to see you even when you have nothing.
sections.heading: The words inside this story

terms.gloss: The home of a bear. It is a cave with a door, and it is warm inside.

terms.gloss: To give part of what you have to someone else, and let them have some too.

terms.gloss: The sad feeling you get when someone else has something you want. It is a feeling, not a plan.

terms.example: A friend brings you a pot of honey in winter.
terms.gloss: Someone who is glad to see you, even when you have nothing to give.

sections.body:
What did Bo learn? Bo learned that keeping everything can make you the loneliest one of all. And he learned that people often give quietly, without telling you.

That is a good thing to remember. Look at your friends. Say thank you out loud, before the snow comes.

Here is how to tell this story to someone. Keep the order, and the surprise will land in the right place.

Start with who the story is about. Tell the problem in the middle. Save the surprise for last. Then say the small lesson in one short sentence.

The lesson of this story is this: sharing makes you richer, not poorer.
examples: The story starts with a bear and twelve honey pots.
The surprise comes at the end.
Sharing makes you richer, not poorer.
sections.heading: The small lesson, and how to tell the story
steps: Start by naming the character: Bo the bear and his twelve honey pots.
Tell the problem: Bo says no to every friend.
Tell the middle: winter comes and Bo has nothing.
End with the surprise and the lesson: sharing makes you richer.

item.summary: A bear keeps every pot of honey for himself, and says no to all his friends. Follow him through autumn into the cold winter, when his friends share with him instead. After reading, you can retell the story, use its new words, and tell its lesson about sharing.
item.title: The Bear Who Learned to Share
